claims.feature: dialogue preserved as far as possible
claims.claim: Tiller promised Tolkien that the dialogue of the original book would be preserved as far as possible, with a narrator linking scenes and cutting preferred to summarising.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)

claims.claim: Tiller admitted that a great deal of the flavour of the work had been lost through telescoping incidents, and Tolkien replied he did not think more could have been done in the time.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
claims.quote: a great deal of the flavour

claims.claim: Tolkien rejected the expectation that hobbits should pipe and squeak, asking why tones should rise with fall in stature, and judged the Elves managed excellently, the Council of Elrond masterly, and Bilbo bored.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
claims.quote: Why should tones rise with fall in stature?

claims.claim: Tolkien liked Glóin's accent but found it heavily laid on, noting dwarves spoke the Common Tongue natively with a uvular back R.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)

claims.claim: A 1955 review held that Tolkien's relaxed, vivid and masculine style with its rich coinages adapted naturally to radio and held attention even when expository.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)

claims.claim: Listeners to the compressed Series Two called it an absolute ruin and a farce whose ignominious compression produced a juvenile adventure story.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
claims.quote: footling and ridiculous sounding adventure story

claims.claim: Tolkien described Norman Shelley's Bombadil as dreadful and the announcer's misdescription of Goldberry and Willowman as worse still (Letters 175, 176, 198).
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)

claims.claim: The 1979 Mind's Eye version removed much back history and expository narration and, with lines recorded separately, produced curiously stilted exchanges of dialogue and frequent mispronunciations.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings — The Mind's Eye Radio Adaptation (1979) (Contains Moderate Peril)

claims.claim: Wikipedia notes the Virginia theatre players of the 1979 adaptation had difficulty pronouncing the names of characters and places, though the version kept Tom Bombadil.
claims.source: The Lord of the Rings (1979 radio series) (Wikipedia)

claims.claim: The 2017 Tolkien: Medieval and Modern post argues Jackson replaced Tolkien's speech-register distinctions (rustic hobbits, more antique Gondor and Rohan) with visual accents, turning Gandalf's conditional syntax into the flat 'The Ring is altogether evil'.
claims.source: How Peter Jackson's Movies Fail to Adapt Tolkien's Style (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2017)

claims.claim: The same post holds that Jackson introduces ironic mockery of characters, a mode Tolkien never uses, and cuts nearly all verse that distinguished the peoples.
claims.source: How Peter Jackson's Movies Fail to Adapt Tolkien's Style (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2017)

claims.claim: Croft's 'Mithril Coats and Tin Ears' argues Jackson and Zimmerman flattened Tolkien's characters, dialogue and plot and showed too much too soon.

Kullmann and Siepmann's corpus study shows Aragorn archaic with inversions, Sam colloquial and politely hedged, Gandalf plain and commanding, Legolas and Gimli proverbial, and Gollum an idiolect of obsessive repetition and minimal syntax.
Walker finds Tolkien uses few actually archaic words yet achieves a nostalgic, maybe even archaic essence through words like 'deem', 'moot', 'wight' and 'westering'.
Turner shows Tolkien's paratactic 'and'-linked sentences at key moments create an impression of exalted register through biblical association without archaic vocabulary.

verdicts.trueWording: Tiller: 'the dialogue of the original book would be preserved as far as possible'
verdicts.note: Lee, p.2: Tiller's 2/2/55 reply carries the quote verbatim; 'A Narrator would be used to link scenes'; 'Cutting would be necessary... but he preferred this to excessive summarising'. Every limb on the raw PDF text.

verdicts.trueWording: 'inevitably a great deal of the flavour of your work has been lost'
verdicts.note: Raw PDF: Tiller 21/9/55 quote verbatim, then 'Tiller had therefore telescope[d] incidents'; Tolkien 27/9/55: 'I do not think that with the time at your disposal you could have done any better'.

verdicts.trueWording: 'Why should tones rise with fall in stature?'
verdicts.note: Raw PDF: quote verbatim; same sentence carries Hobbits should 'pipe and squeak', Elves 'managed excellently', Council of Elrond 'masterly', Bilbo sounded 'bored'. All five limbs present.

verdicts.trueWording: 'heavily laid on'; 'dwarves spoke the Common Tongue natively... uvular back R'
verdicts.note: Raw PDF: 'He liked Gloin's accent but added it was a bit heavily laid on noting dwarves spoke the Common Tongue natively, like Jews, but they had a uvular back R'. Claim omits 'like Jews' but adds nothing unsupported.

verdicts.trueWording: 'relaxed, vivid, and masculine style with its rich coinages'
verdicts.note: Raw PDF: uncatalogued clipping review 'The Meaning of the Ring' 15/11/55 (so 1955); 'adapted naturally to radio'; 'holds the attention even when he is being expository'.

Raw PDF: all four phrases in one sentence about Series Two; the claim's quote field 'footling and ridiculous sounding adventure story' is also verbatim in the following Civil Servant listener comment.

Raw PDF footnote 2: Letters #175 (Molly Waldron 30/11/55) carries both quotes; the same footnote cites Letters #176 and #198. Note: #176/#198 are cited as further references, not as the source of the two quoted phrases.

verdicts.trueWording: 'some curiously stilted exchanges of dialogue in key scenes'
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'much of the back history, lore and expositionary narration removed'; 'the cast often recorded their lines separately resulting in some curiously stilted exchanges'; 'The pronunciation of many names and places are often incorrect'.

verdicts.trueWording: 'had difficulty pronouncing the names of characters and places'
verdicts.note: Raw Wikipedia text: that phrase is word for word (attributed there to the SF-Worlds review of the local Virginia theater players); the article separately says it is 'notable for including the Tom Bombadil scenes'.

verdicts.trueWording: Post says Jackson uses accents 'immersing them in the sounds'
verdicts.note: Register limbs all verbatim: Appendix F 'hobbits indeed spoke for the most part a rustic dialect, whereas in Gondor and Rohan a more antique language was used'; 'Jackson uses accents to convey these differences instead'; the conditional-syntax contrast and the film line 'The Ring is altogether evil' are both on the page (dated April 11, 2017).
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: Accents called 'visual' - the post treats accents as auditory ('immersing them in the sounds of Middle Earth'), explicitly distinct from the films' visuals

verdicts.trueWording: Tolkien 'never operates on an ironic level'; 'verse is very rarely present'
verdicts.note: Raw page: movies 'take multiple breaks to laugh at characters, mainly Merry, Pippin, or Gimli'; 'Tolkien never poked direct fun at the characters'; poems 'distinguish the different races of Middle Earth' yet verse is very rarely present in Jackson. Claim is paraphrase, not quotation (empty quote field).

verdicts.trueWording: Croft argues both men 'flatten[ed]' Tolkien's characters, dialogue, and plot
verdicts.note: Raw Wikipedia text of the Mithril Coats and Tin Ears row: 'both men' = Jackson and Morton Zimmerman; 'too much too soon' is supported by 'where Tolkien subtly builds tension, Jackson habit[ually] gives away what will happen' and the essay's 'Anticipation'. The page renders the quoted word with a bracketed inflection, 'flatten[ed]'.

verdicts.trueWording: Gollum's 'extraordinary idiolect' is Rosebury's phrase, not theirs
verdicts.note: The Fellowship table 'after Kullmann and Siepmann' supports five limbs exactly: Aragorn Archaic/literary with Inversion; Sam Colloquial, rustic, working class, 'Often politely hedged'; Gandalf Plain, flexible, Commands; Gimli and Legolas Literary with Proverbs. Kullmann and Siepmann's corpus linguistics is also stated. But Gollum is outside the table and outside their attribution.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: Gollum's idiolect of obsessive repetition and minimal syntax - the page attributes that to Brian Rosebury; Kullmann and Siepmann are cited only for Gollum's 'non-standard speech'

verdicts.trueWording: 'only a few actually archaic words'; 'nostalgic, maybe even archaic'
verdicts.note: Raw Wikipedia text, Syntax and diction: Walker on 'only a few actually archaic words'; diction 'manages to seem in its essence nostalgic, maybe even archaic'; and antiquity coming from 'deem', 'moot', 'wight' combined with still-current 'darkling' and 'westering'.

verdicts.trueWording: readers experience it as 'an impression of exalted register'
verdicts.note: Raw Wikipedia text: Turner on the Pelennor eucatastrophe passage - paratactic style with repeated 'and' 'in the manner of the New Testament', the impression arising 'because of the biblical association'; Turner's 'special stylistic effects at key moments' supports the key-moments limb. The page says Tolkien uses 'few unusual or archaic words' there rather than none.
